title: Predistribution at Work
abstract: An occupation-blind income tax distorts workers toward higher-amenity jobs by taxing compensating differentials. Using a multidimensional Mirrleesian framework with job amenities, I derive two results. First, predistribution that improves conditions in disamenable jobs is desirable due to a fiscal externality: it induces workers to reallocate toward low-amenity occupations, earning compensating differentials that are taxed. The inability to condition taxes on occupation breaks the Atkinson-Stiglitz theorem and justifies labor market interventions on fiscal grounds alone. Second, accounting for this distortion lowers optimal taxes. A calibration to U.S. data finds that compensating differentials lower optimal marginal tax rates by one to four percentage points. Even coarsely applied to the worst jobs, predistribution acts as implicit occupational targeting and internalizes the fiscal externality far more effectively than tax reductions alone.
